newsitem.title: USA: Coffee up on squeeze worry, corn and soy rise.
newsitem.headline: Coffee up on squeeze worry, corn and soy rise.

text.p: Coffee prices jumped to the highest levels in six weeks on Monday as speculators and commercial coffee firms bought on concerns about a shortage of coffee in warehouses available for delivery against futures.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for September delivery closed 12.05 cents a pound higher at 188.35 cents, up nearly seven percent on the day and the highest closing price since June 17.

"There is renewed talk of tightness in September," said Merrill Lynch market analyst Judith Ganes, noting that the number of contracts in the September futures still open for delivery was unusally large.
"Open interest is high, stocks are low and there's not much coffee coming in to offset it," Ganes said.

After Monday's close, the exchange reported that the amount of coffee in warehouses certified for delivery against futures fell by 750 132-pound bags as of July 25 to a total 92,078 bags -- the equivalent of about 328 futures contracts.
Meanwhile, the amount of open interest or contracts still open for trading in the September futures stood at 11,512 lots as of Friday.
So fear of a possible "squeeze" on those holding large short or selling positions in futures has risen. Cash deliveries against the September coffee contract begin on August 21.

"September is the most squeezable month because its delivery is ahead of the Colombian main crop and there's nothing out of Central America," said one New York dealer. "Everyone needs coffee and there're no milds around," the dealer said.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn and soybean prices rose as weather forecasts for another bout of hot, dry weather in the Midwest overcame a sense of relief that rains fell over the weekend in growing areas of Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa.
Soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November closed 18 cents a bushel higher at $6.19-1/4 while corn for December delivery added 8-3/4 cents a bushel to close at $2.52.
Meteorologists said weekend storms brought 0.10 to 0.50 inch with about 20 percent coverage in central Illinois. The trade had expected heavier rainfall and wider coverage.

"The weather left something to be desired," said Vic Lespinasse, trader with Dean Witter. "We didn't get as much rain as we thought and there's very little rain in the forecast. It's going to be cooler for a few days but then it's going to heat up again toward the end of the week."
Both corn and soybean are in crucial stages of growth at the present time, with heat stress and lack of moisture likely to cut into the expected bumper crops if hot conditions persist.

Wheat for December delivery closed down 1-1/2 cents a bushel at $3.70-1/2 following news that Egypt bought only 200,000 metric tons of wheat from the United States at a weekend tender. Some traders had expected a purchase of 500,000 tons or more.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, the price of gasoline for August delivery closed 0.81 cent a gallon higher at 64.84 cents on concerns about tight supplies.
But most other oil-related contracts closed lower on news that Iraq was finally nearing United Nations's approval for a second round of "oil-for-food" sales.
Crude oil for September delivery fell 8 cents a barrel at $19.81 and heating oil for September delivery fell 0.13 cent a gallon at 54.51 cents.
"The main factor here is that gasoline continues to be the leader of the market," said Gerald Samuels, managing director of Arb Oil. "It's pretty much a one-horse show," he added.

Strength in the price of the "reformulated" gasoline deliverable on the exchange has largely been caused by the high price of methyl butyl tertiary ether (MTBE), which has suffered production problems over the past several week.
MTBE is a blending component for reformulated gasoline.
